findings.issue_text: [BUG] The MaxAge cleanup loop calls r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ... "err", err) on every successful batch, logging at error level with a nil err and the full ID slice. Every annotation cleanup cycle (now running every minute per cleanup.go) emits error-level log spam including up to batchSize IDs per batch to operators' logs, polluting error dashboards and making real errors indistinguishable from routine progress.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup loop calls r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by count", ... "err", err) on every successful batch with a nil err and the full ID slice. Error-level noise per batch on every cycle, sent to operators' error log streams; with a large backlog this is thousands of error-severity lines per run with no actual error.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs r.log.Error("Tags to clean", ...) and r.log.Error("cleaned tags", ...) for every successful batch, including a nil "err". Routine orphan-tag cleanup progress is reported as errors in production logs, at a now-minute cadence, with the full tag ID list inline.

[ADVISORY] deleteByIDs is called with the result of fetchIDs but its error variable y is logged with the value from the fetch branch shadowed — specifically `x, y := r.deleteByIDs(...)` then `r.log.Error(..., "err", y)` returns y correctly, but the preceding log of "err", err inside the same callback logs the nil fetch error, so no real signal is distinguishable. The next maintainer debugging cleanup failures gets two adjacent error-level lines per batch with nil errors, obscuring which operation actually failed; change-safety of this code is degraded.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup job ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no config gate, which is a 10x increase in the frequency of all registered cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup. Every cleanup job implementing Run (including any that do expensive scans) now runs 10x more often in all Grafana deployments; operators who tuned jobs against the 10-minute cadence see increased background DB load, and the change cannot be reverted without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] fetchIDs rejects an empty condition but deleteByIDs silently returns (0, nil) for empty ids, so untilDoneOrCancelled's termination relies solely on the loop's affected==0 check rather than an explicit done signal, duplicating termination knowledge between the helper and its callers. A future caller whose batchWork can delete zero rows while more work remains (e.g., rows skipped due to concurrent-insert under-deletion noted in the comment) terminates the loop early; the next maintainer changing delete semantics can silently truncate cleanup.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite >999-ID path interpolates IDs via fmt.Sprintf into the SQL string while the parameterized branch sits beside it, a parallel code path exercised only when batchSize > 999 on SQLite — and the new test only covers it via the 32767-batch case, leaving the boundary (batchSize exactly 999/1000) and non-SQLite placeholder branch with batchSize > 999 untested. A regression in either branch (e.g., off-by-one in the placeholder count `strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)` with len 1, which yields "?" correctly but with len 0 is guarded) or in string interpolation would only surface in production on the affected dialect since the test matrix never varies dialect.

[ADVISORY] The new 40003-annotation test sets annotationCleanupJobBatchSize to 32767 and asserts 40000 affected, but the test's name and the const comment in deleteByIDs disagree (comment says SQLite limit is 999; test name references SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER 32767 for SQLite >= 3.32), and the test will use the string-interpolation delete path only if InitTestDB is SQLite, tying the assertion of "should not fail" to an implicit environment assumption. If InitTestDB is configured to a non-SQLite dialect (or the dialect check changes), the test exercises the placeholder path with 32767 parameters, which exceeds MySQL/Postgres driver parameter limits differently and can fail confusingly; the stale 999 comment misleads the next maintainer about which limit actually matters.

[BUG] Routine, successful cleanup batches are logged at Error level via r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...), including the full slice of IDs, in the MaxAge path of CleanAnnotations. Every annotation cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines with potentially thousands of IDs per batch, permanently polluting operator alerting on error-level logs and ballooning log volume; the trailing "err", err field is always nil because the error branch already returned before the log call.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup path logs each successful batch at Error level with r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by count", ...), including the full ID list. Operators paging on error-level logs get spammed every cleanup run; nil error is logged as a field, and the ID slice can contain the full batch size (default-bounded but user-configurable to tens of thousands).

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs every successful batch at Error level (r.log.Error("Tags to clean", ...) / r.log.Error("cleaned tags", ...)) with the full ID slice. Same error-level log spam as the other two sites; on a database with a large orphaned-tag backlog this fires per batch, every minute (see ticker change), producing continuous false-positive error alerts.

[BUG] deleteByIDs only special-cases the SQLite 999-parameter limit; the placeholder path is used unconditionally on Postgres and MySQL regardless of batch size, and Postgres's wire-protocol bind limit (32767 parameters) is not guarded. A user who sets annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size above 32767 on Postgres gets every batch failing with a bind-parameter error ("bind message has N result formats..."), so annotation cleanup stops deleting anything and the cleanup job errors each cycle — the exact failure mode the SQLite workaround was added to prevent, reintroduced for another backend.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval is hard-coded from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no configuration knob and no explanation of why the 10x frequency increase is required. Operators on MySQL/Postgres get the (now error-level, ID-dumping) cleanup logging firing every minute per cleanup service, and the DB runs the annotation/tag cleanup queries 10x more often; the change is baked in and cannot be tuned back without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite fallback inlines the ID list directly into the SQL string via fmt.Sprint/sprintf, producing a raw ~700KB statement for a 32767-ID batch instead of using chunked parameterized deletes (e.g., 999-ID slices). Large batches flirt with SQLite's default max statement length and the raw-SQL path must be audited as a string-built query forever; deleting in 999-parameter chunks would keep parameterization and bounded statement size, deleting the entire dialect branch's raw-SQL construction.

[BUG] The MaxAge cleanup path logs every batch at Error level, including the full slice of IDs and a nil err, on the success path. Every cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default large, and this diff explicitly supports 32767) IDs per batch, flooding error logs/alerting on healthy runs and dumping huge ID lists into logs; operators monitoring ERROR see constant noise and cannot distinguish real failures.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup path logs every batch at Error level with the full ID list and nil err on success. Same as the MaxAge site: error-level log spam with potentially tens of thousands of IDs per batch on every healthy cleanup run, poisoning ERROR-level monitoring and making genuine cleanup failures indistinguishable from normal operation.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs each batch at Error level with the ID list, count, cond, and a nil err even when deletion succeeds. Orphaned-tag cleanup runs every cycle and unconditionally writes error-severity log lines with full ID slices; a large orphan backlog (the exact scenario this PR optimizes) produces megabytes of ERROR logs and pages on-call for a successful operation.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no requirement in the stated intent (database performance optimizations) explaining it. All registered cleanup jobs run 10x more often against the database; operators of large deployments get a 10x increase in background DB churn from this PR alone, and the change is invisible/undocumented relative to the PR's stated scope — a future reader cannot trace it to any requirement or config knob (it cannot be tuned without a code deploy).

[ADVISORY] The new fetchIDs helper takes a raw table name and condition interpolated via fmt.Sprintf, an API surface broader than any requirement in this PR demands. Both call sites build SQL by string-formatting table and condition fragments with no escaping or validation; the next contributor adding a cleanup path gets an easy SQL-injection-by-string-concatenation footgun (any condition value interpolated from user-influenced config), where the deleted code built queries in one closed site. This widens the trusted-input surface beyond what the deadlocking-fix requirement needed.

[BUG] Normal-path cleanup diagnostics are emitted at log.Error level, including the full ID slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries) on every successful batch, duplicated at 6 call sites across CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags. Every cleanup cycle on every Grafana instance writes ERROR-level entries containing thousands of IDs ('Annotations to clean by time', 'count', 'ids', ...) even when nothing failed — operators see constant errors in logs, error-rate alerting fires on healthy systems, and the id-list payload bloats logs proportional to batch size; err is also logged even though it is always nil on this path, making the messages indistinguishable from real failures.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval was cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute while the annotation cleanup work per cycle grew (each batch is now a SELECT plus a DELETE instead of one statement), with no config option to tune it. Database load from the cleanup job increases roughly 10x in query frequency and 2x in statement count per batch; deployments with large annotation tables now run the fetchIDs scan every minute, and operators cannot restore the previous cadence without a code change since the interval is hardcoded.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite fallback in deleteByIDs builds the IN-list via repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation (values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)), which is O(n²) in the number of IDs. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize set high (the test uses 32767), each batch re-copies a string that grows to hundreds of kilobytes ~n times — measurable CPU churn in the cleanup path on SQLite deployments; strings.Builder or a single pre-sized join makes this O(n).

[ADVISORY] The SQLite parameter-limit workaround branches on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, but the non-SQLite path passes all batch IDs as placeholders with no bound on their count, coupling the dialect-specific limit knowledge (999 for SQLite) into deleteByIDs as a magic number while other dialects' variable limits (e.g. SQL Server's 2100) are unguarded. A user on a non-SQLite backend who sets AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above their driver's parameter limit (SQL Server ~2100, Postgres 32767 for ints) gets a hard runtime error from the cleanup job every cycle; the check tests the config value rather than the actual placeholder count, and the limit constants are scattered rather than centralized in the dialect layer.

[BUG] CleanAnnotations logs every batch's candidate IDs at Error level, including the full ID slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 IDs) and an always-nil err, on both the MaxAge and MaxCount paths. Every cleanup cycle (now every 1 minute) emits Error-level log lines containing thousands of IDs on a healthy system, flooding logs with false errors and megabytes of ID lists for any instance with old annotations — operators' error dashboards and alerting on error-level logs fill with noise.

[BUG] The MaxCount branch logs the same debug payload (full ID slice plus nil err) at Error level. Same log-flood failure mode as the MaxAge path; also the logged 'err' field is always nil, so anyone triaging these Error lines is misled into thinking a deletion failed when it succeeded.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs 'Tags to clean' / 'cleaned tags' at Error level with the full ID list and a nil err. A routine, successful tag-cleanup batch appears as an error in production logs with thousands of tag IDs, polluting error-rate metrics and log storage every minute on instances with orphaned tags.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup job ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without any config knob or migration note, silently altering the job's scheduling contract. All Grafana instances now run the full annotation/tag cleanup scan 10x more often; large deployments with big annotation tables see 10x the background DB load (fetch-IDs queries plus delete batches) with no way to tune it back without a code change.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup path logs every batch's full ID list and raw SQL condition at Error level (r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)), on both success and failure, in every batch of every cleanup cycle. Operators running with AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize in the thousands (the new large-batch mode this diff adds) get every annotation ID emitted at Error severity once per minute (the ticker was also cut from 10min to 1min), flooding logs, tripping log-based alerting on "error" messages for a routine job, and dumping internal query structure into general log storage where it may be shipped to third-party log aggregators.

[ADVISORY] The success path logs a nil error and zero-count information via r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ... "err", y) — an Error-level call with "err" bound to nil and no failure occurred. Anyone monitoring Grafana logs for errors (SREs, log scanners, on-call) sees continuous 'Error' entries from the annotation cleaner during normal operation, masking real errors in alerting rules that key on error-level logs.

[BUG] The new cleanup loop logs every batch at Error level via r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...) even on success, with err always nil at that point. Every scheduled cleanup cycle (now running every minute per cleanup.go's ticker change) emits error-level logs containing the full list of deleted annotation IDs — operators see a stream of false 'error' alerts in production, and the ID list can contain up to 32767 entries per line, bloating logs. The 'err' key is always nil, so the log entry is also misleading.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup path repeats the same misleveled r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by count", "ids", ids, ...) call per batch with a nil error. Same false-error log spam on every one-minute cleanup tick for deployments using maxCount cleanup; error dashboards alert on successful routine work.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs 'Tags to clean' / 'cleaned tags' at Error level with the full ID slice on every batch. Every orphaned-tag cleanup batch produces an error-severity log line with potentially thousands of IDs, polluting error monitoring and log storage each cleanup run.

[ADVISORY] The stated purpose of the refactor — avoiding MySQL deadlocks with concurrent inserts by allowing locks to flush between the ID fetch and the delete — is not exercised by any test in this diff (checked pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/cleanup_test.go, the only test file touched). The deadlock fix itself is verified only by the author's manual MySQL observation; all diff tests run against SQLite (db.InitTestDB), which neither exhibits the MySQL lock behavior nor runs concurrent inserts during cleanup. A regression that reintroduces the single-statement subquery (or breaks the session-scoping that lets locks flush) passes the entire new suite; only a production MySQL deployment with concurrent annotation writes gets bitten.

[ADVISORY] The new 40003-annotation case is the only test that exercises the SQLite inline-ID branch of deleteByIDs (r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999 && SQLite), but it only asserts final counts — it never asserts that the batch actually split into multiple delete rounds or that the inline (non-placeholder) SQL path was taken rather than the placeholder path with a small effective batch. If the SQLite special-case threshold logic regresses (e.g. the comparison flips to >=, or fetchIDs silently clamps to fewer than 1000 IDs so the placeholder path always runs), the test still passes because the loop terminates on zero-affected regardless of which branch executed; the SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER failure mode the test name promises to guard resurfaces only when a real user configures a batch size over the limit on SQLite with >999 rows matching.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten untilDoneOrCancelled now interleaves two separate session operations (fetchIDs + deleteByIDs) per iteration, so the context-cancellation window between a successful fetch and the delete (and after partial totalAffected accumulation) has no test coverage — the existing tests only exercise the happy path to completion. A context cancelled mid-batch now returns partial totalAffected plus ctx.Err() from a point between two queries rather than inside one; nothing in the diff verifies the caller (CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags and their callers in cleanup.go) handles this partial-count + error combination correctly, and the new fetch step's error path (fetchIDs failing after earlier successful deletes) is never triggered by any test.

[ADVISORY] The new batched cleanup logs every batch at Error level via r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..."ids", ids...) even on fully successful runs, dumping the entire fetched ID list (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32k IDs) into error logs twice per batch. Operators with error-log alerting get paged/flooded on every routine successful cleanup run; on a large instance the log volume is 2x batchSize IDs per batch per cycle, and nil errors logged as "err" make triage misleading.

[ADVISORY] The MaxCount cleanup branch logs each batch at Error level with the full ids slice and a nil err, same defect as the MaxAge branch. Same error-severity log flood on successful runs; conflates healthy cleanup with real errors in alerting.

[ADVISORY] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs each batch at Error level with the full orphaned-tag ID list and nil err on the success path. Error-log alerting noise and large log volume per cleanup cycle for a routine, successful operation.

[ADVISORY] untilDoneOrCancelled treats a batch that fetched IDs but deleted 0 rows (e.g. rows removed by a concurrent cleanup process or overlapping instance between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, which run in separate sessions) as 'done' and exits the loop early, conflating 'nothing to fetch' with 'nothing deleted'. A single lost race truncates that cleanup pass, leaving annotations/tags that meet the deletion criteria in place until the next cycle; with the MaxCount rule this means retention limits are transiently violated. Self-healing on the next run, but the termination signal is wrong.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, a 10x increase in frequency of the annotation cleanup queries, which this diff also makes heavier (each batch is now two round trips: a SELECT id fetch plus a DELETE). Every Grafana instance now runs the fetch+delete cleanup queries 10x more often; instances with large annotation tables that previously absorbed one scan per 10 minutes now run ~2880 batched query pairs per day, increasing steady-state DB load with no feature flag to tune the interval.

[BUG] Cleanup progress is logged at Error level with an always-nil `err` field, so every successful cleanup batch emits an error-severity log line. Operators running annotation cleanup see recurring `logger=annotations.cleanup level=error msg="Annotations to clean by time" err=null` lines (five such sites in CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags, each also dumping the full ids slice, up to batch-size entries, and the SQL condition). On a large cleanup this floods error logs and alerting on level=error, and the logged `err` field can never contain a real error at these sites because `fetchIDs` errors are returned before the log statement executes — the line misdirects debugging toward a nil error during incident triage.

[ADVISORY] Every cleanup batch logs the complete fetched ID slice at Error level, producing log lines whose size grows linearly with AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default unbounded up to 32k+ IDs per line in the new SQLite test configuration). Grafana operators with large annotation tables get multi-megabyte log lines every cleanup cycle; log shippers/aggregators (Loki, Elastic) ingest the full ID list that has no diagnostic value. Counter-argument: 'it aids debugging deletion counts' — the count field already carries that, and the per-ID list is reproducible from the DB, so the finding survives.

[ADVISORY] Cleanup job ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no corresponding config, multiplying background DB load (annotation ID fetch + delete batches, orphan tag scan) by 10x on every Grafana instance. Every Grafana deployment now runs the annotation cleanup queries and tmp-file sweep twelve times more often; instances with cleanup disabled via 0/0 settings still pay the job-scheduling overhead, and MySQL/Postgres deployments that previously saw the deadlock-prone delete once per 10 minutes now exercise the new fetch+delete path every minute. Counter-argument: 'each run is cheaper now that it's batched' — the batching is per-run, not amortizing the fixed scan cost, so frequency dominates; finding survives as a load regression to flag, though severity is low.

goldens.comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

This is verifiable from the diff and would generate error-severity log noise (and potentially very large log payloads) on every successful batch, but it does not change functional correctness of cleanup itself.

adjudication.rationale: In the new cleanup loops (e.g., CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags), the code logs with r.log.Error(..., "err", err) immediately after fetchIDs succeeds (meaning err is necessarily nil due to the prior `if err != nil { return ... }`). This produces error-level log lines with nil errors and can obscure real failures in subsequent operations. However, the finding’s claim about error-variable shadowing is not accurate: `x, y := r.deleteByIDs(...)` uses a different variable (`y`) and returns it correctly; there’s no shadowing bug affecting correctness—this is primarily a misleading/over-severe logging concern introduced by the diff.

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `untilDoneOrCancelled` stops when the batch callback returns `affected == 0` (see new helper in `xorm_store.go`). All current callers compute `ids := r.fetchIDs(...)` and then call `r.deleteByIDs(...)`, where `deleteByIDs` explicitly returns `(0, nil)` when `len(ids) == 0`. So the “done” signal is implicitly encoded as “0 affected”, not an explicit sentinel, and the loop termination contract is spread across `untilDoneOrCancelled` and each `batchWork` implementation. While this is not a concrete defect for the shown usages (they fetch IDs each iteration and delete them), it is a real maintainability/edge-case concern: if a future `batchWork` can legitimately return 0 affected while more work remains (e.g., due to races where fetched IDs are gone by delete time, or changed delete semantics), the loop would terminate early without error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces two distinct code paths in deleteByIDs(): a SQLite-only branch that interpolates IDs into the SQL string when DBType is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, and a parameterized placeholders branch otherwise. The added integration test exercises the SQLite interpolation path via batchSize=32767, but the diff does not add coverage for the boundary around 999 (exactly 999 vs 1000) nor for the non-SQLite placeholders branch when batch size is large (since the branch condition is dialect-dependent). This is a concrete, diff-grounded testing gap for newly added nontrivial branching logic, not a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new 40003-annotation test sets annotationCleanupJobBatchSize to 32767 and asserts 40000 affected, but the test's name and the const comment in deleteByIDs disagree (comment says SQLite limit is 999; test name references SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER 32767 for SQLite >= 3.32), and the test will use the string-interpolation delete path only if InitTestDB is SQLite, tying the assertion of "should not fail" to an implicit environment assumption. If InitTestDB is configured to a non-SQLite dialect (or the dialect check changes), the test exercises the placeholder path with 32767 parameters, which exceeds MySQL/Postgres driver parameter limits differently and can fail confusingly; the stale 999 comment misleads the next maintainer about which limit actually matters.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows an inconsistency and potential test fragility rather than a clear functional defect. The new integration test case is named around SQLite’s `SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER` (32767) and sets `annotationCleanupJobBatchSize: 32767`, but the production code comment and branch condition in `deleteByIDs` hardcode a `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` and switch to string-interpolated `IN (...)` deletes when `dbtype == SQLite && batchSize > 999`. That mismatch is real in the diff and can mislead maintainers. Also, the test’s intent (“should not fail... for SQLite”) implicitly depends on `db.InitTestDB(t)` using SQLite; if it runs against a non-SQLite dialect, the code will take the placeholder path with 32767 parameters (`placeholders := "?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)`), which could hit driver/DB parameter limits, making the test environment-sensitive.

Every annotation cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines with potentially thousands of IDs per batch, permanently polluting operator alerting on error-level logs and ballooning log volume; the trailing "err", err field is always nil because the error branch already returned before the log call.

adjudication.rationale: In `CleanAnnotations` the new batching logic logs routine successful work at error level and includes the full `ids` slice: e.g. in the MaxAge path it does `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` immediately after `fetchIDs` succeeds. If `fetchIDs` had errored, the function returns before the log, so the logged `err` is always nil. This will emit error-level logs on every cleanup batch and can dump thousands of IDs per batch, unnecessarily polluting error logs and increasing log volume. The same pattern exists in the MaxCount and orphan-tag cleanup paths.

Operators paging on error-level logs get spammed every cleanup run; nil error is logged as a field, and the ID slice can contain the full batch size (default-bounded but user-configurable to tens of thousands).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] deleteByIDs only special-cases the SQLite 999-parameter limit; the placeholder path is used unconditionally on Postgres and MySQL regardless of batch size, and Postgres's wire-protocol bind limit (32767 parameters) is not guarded. A user who sets annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size above 32767 on Postgres gets every batch failing with a bind-parameter error ("bind message has N result formats..."), so annotation cleanup stops deleting anything and the cleanup job errors each cycle — the exact failure mode the SQLite workaround was added to prevent, reintroduced for another backend.

adjudication.rationale: In `deleteByIDs`, non-SQLite backends always use the placeholder path (`?, ?, ...`) with one bind parameter per ID (via `placeholders := "?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)` and `args = asAny(ids)`). The number of IDs comes directly from `fetchIDs` which applies `Limit(r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize)`, so a user-configured large `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` will generate a statement with that many bind parameters on Postgres/MySQL. The diff only guards SQLite’s low parameter limit (999) and provides no analogous cap/chunking for other DBs, so on backends with bind/parameter limits this can cause batch execution errors and prevent cleanup from progressing.

Large batches flirt with SQLite's default max statement length and the raw-SQL path must be audited as a string-built query forever; deleting in 999-parameter chunks would keep parameterization and bounded statement size, deleting the entire dialect branch's raw-SQL construction.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite fallback in deleteByIDs builds the IN-list via repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation (values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)), which is O(n²) in the number of IDs. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize set high (the test uses 32767), each batch re-copies a string that grows to hundreds of kilobytes ~n times — measurable CPU churn in the cleanup path on SQLite deployments; strings.Builder or a single pre-sized join makes this O(n).

adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go deleteByIDs(), the SQLite branch constructs the IN-list by repeatedly rebuilding a growing string: `values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])` then `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Given the diff also adds a test with `annotationCleanupJobBatchSize: 32767`, this can become a noticeable CPU/memory churn on SQLite. It’s a performance concern, not a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite parameter-limit workaround branches on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, but the non-SQLite path passes all batch IDs as placeholders with no bound on their count, coupling the dialect-specific limit knowledge (999 for SQLite) into deleteByIDs as a magic number while other dialects' variable limits (e.g. SQL Server's 2100) are unguarded. A user on a non-SQLite backend who sets AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above their driver's parameter limit (SQL Server ~2100, Postgres 32767 for ints) gets a hard runtime error from the cleanup job every cycle; the check tests the config value rather than the actual placeholder count, and the limit constants are scattered rather than centralized in the dialect layer.

adjudication.rationale: In `deleteByIDs`, the code special-cases only SQLite via a hard-coded `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` and otherwise builds a placeholder list sized to `len(ids)` (`"?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)`) and passes all IDs as parameters. Since `ids` is fetched with a `LIMIT` equal to `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize`, a large configured batch size can produce a statement with that many parameters on non-SQLite DBs, with no guard or dialect-specific cap. This is a real, diff-grounded robustness/portability concern introduced by switching from single-statement deletes to ID-list deletes, but the diff alone doesn’t prove it breaks on Grafana’s supported DBs in default configs (it depends on backend limits and user configuration).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The stated purpose of the refactor — avoiding MySQL deadlocks with concurrent inserts by allowing locks to flush between the ID fetch and the delete — is not exercised by any test in this diff (checked pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/cleanup_test.go, the only test file touched). Nothing in the diff exercises the MySQL deadlock scenario or verifies that the new “locks flush between batches” behavior is necessary/correct, so a regression back to the prior single-statement approach would still pass these tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new 40003-annotation case is the only test that exercises the SQLite inline-ID branch of deleteByIDs (r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999 && SQLite), but it only asserts final counts — it never asserts that the batch actually split into multiple delete rounds or that the inline (non-placeholder) SQL path was taken rather than the placeholder path with a small effective batch. If the SQLite special-case threshold logic regresses (e.g. the comparison flips to >=, or fetchIDs silently clamps to fewer than 1000 IDs so the placeholder path always runs), the test still passes because the loop terminates on zero-affected regardless of which branch executed; the SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER failure mode the test name promises to guard resurfaces only when a real user configures a batch size over the limit on SQLite with >999 rows matching.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rewritten untilDoneOrCancelled now interleaves two separate session operations (fetchIDs + deleteByIDs) per iteration, so the context-cancellation window between a successful fetch and the delete (and after partial totalAffected accumulation) has no test coverage — the existing tests only exercise the happy path to completion. The updated integration tests in `cleanup_test.go` exercise only successful completion paths (no context cancellation, no induced `fetchIDs` failure after prior batches). That means the newly introduced mid-batch cancellation/error behavior (partial `totalAffected` + non-nil error) is not covered by tests. This is a concrete, diff-grounded missing-coverage issue rather than a provable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] untilDoneOrCancelled treats a batch that fetched IDs but deleted 0 rows (e.g. rows removed by a concurrent cleanup process or overlapping instance between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, which run in separate sessions) as 'done' and exits the loop early, conflating 'nothing to fetch' with 'nothing deleted'. Self-healing on the next run, but the termination signal is wrong.

adjudication.rationale: In the new cleanup strategy, each batch does `ids, err := r.fetchIDs(...)` and then returns `x, y := r.deleteByIDs(..., ids)` to `untilDoneOrCancelled`. The loop in `untilDoneOrCancelled` terminates when `affected == 0`. Because `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs` run in separate DB sessions, it’s possible under concurrency that `fetchIDs` returns a non-empty `ids` slice but all those rows are deleted by another process before `deleteByIDs` executes, yielding `affected == 0`. In that case the loop exits even though there may still be additional matching rows beyond this batch (e.g., more old annotations/tags or rows beyond the MaxCount offset), so the cleanup pass can end prematurely. Termination should be based on `len(ids)==0` (nothing left to fetch), not `affected==0` (nothing deleted).
